title: Gemini Decisions API
content:
Gemini Decisions API

Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file:

dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it?
robot: Does this video have a robot in it?
france: Is this video set in France?
usa: Is this video set in the USA?

Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that:

{
  "dragon": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.04976021841520312
  },
  "robot": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.9234055387792485
  },
  "france": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.08329171353166241
  },
  "usa": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.9230459995157706
  }
}

Via Hacker News

Tags: ai, generative-ai, gemini, llm-release, jev, decision-models

title: Semafor: ‘Nvidia Board Preparing to Oust CEO Jensen Huang, Name Interim CEO’
content:
Rohan Goswami, Reed Albergotti, and Ashley Gold, reporting for Semafor at 10:27pm ET:

Some members of Nvidia’s board favor appointing Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO at the beleaguered chipmaker if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people familiar with the matter.

Here’s Kress’s LinkedIn profile.

Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huangas soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official.

Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the company’s next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to another person familiar with the matter.

Kara Swisher spitballed Tim Cook as an idea, but that’s nonsense. If Cook wanted to be the CEO of a Fortune 2 company, he’d still be CEO at Apple. Apple despises Nvidia and Nvidia despises Apple. Cook may well be enjoying this fiasco, but only as entertainment drizzled with fresh farm-to-table schadenfreude — not as a personal opportunity.

Srouji, though, is an interesting name. Semafor doesn’t say whether this is just wishful thinking on the part of Nvidia’s board or if Srouji has indicated receptiveness. Srouji has been at Apple since 2008 but he’s a bit of a cipher. My spidey-sense can’t tell if he bleeds six colors or not.

Mark Gurman — and no one else — claimed last year that Srouji went to Tim Cook and threatened to leave for another company. Srouji called bullshit on this with a memo that stated flatly, “I love my job at Apple, and I don’t plan on leaving anytime soon.” Then, in April, when John Ternus was named Cook’s successor, Srouji was simultaneously promoted to the new position of Chief Hardware Officer.

So one scenario is that Srouji feels no allegiance to Apple, and Tim Cook and John Ternus are the sort of leaders who, when faced with a threat from a subordinate, give in because they’re cowards, and give a big promotion to someone who might leave Apple for a rival just weeks after Apple’s CEO transition.

Another scenario is that Srouji meant what he said, loves his job at Apple, and truly is John Ternus’s trusted and trustworthy hardware lieutenant. In this case, Nvidia’s board leaking that they’re considering Srouji to replace Huang is like someone in hell saying they’re considering ordering some ice water. My money is on this scenario.

 ★

title: I didn’t write a program with emoji, but I did use a control character
content:
Adventures in PC Emulation recently wrote about Executable Emoji: Writing an MS-DOS program using machine code represented solely by Unicode emoji characters.

This reminded me that back in the day I did something similar, but much less impressive: I wrote a reboot.com program that could be generated from the command line via echo.

echo Alt+Num2,Num0,Num5Ctrl+Y>reboot.com

The Alt+Num2,Num0,Num5 means to press and hold the Alt while sequentially pressing and releasing Num2, Num0, Num5 on the numeric keypad, and then releasing the Alt key. In the IBM PC 437 code page, this comes out looking like ═, which is character 205, or hex 0xCD.

The byte 0xCD is the machine code for the int instruction, for issuing a software interrupt. And Ctrl+Y generates character 25, or hex 0x19, which completes the instruction: int 19h.

Interrupt 19h was a sort-of not-very-good “reboot the system” interrupt. You can read about all the problems it has in Ralph Brown’s Interrupt List.

This interrupt reboots the system without clearing memory or restoring interrupt vectors. Because interrupt vectors are preserved, this interrupt usually causes a system hang if any TSRs have hooked vectors from 00h through 1Ch, particularly INT 08.

Since this was not a very good way of rebooting the system, it was mostly just a parlor trick.

But at least I did it.

The post I didn’t write a program with emoji, but I did use a control character appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: Possible Futures
content:
Contents

Click on the blue boxes to go to the corresponding section:

<?xml version=”1.0” encoding=”UTF-8” standalone=”no”?> <!DOCTYPE svg PUBLIC “-//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN” “http://www.w3.org/Graphics/SVG/1.1/DTD/svg11.dtd”>

Questions

  • Do we reach ASI? Do we reach the point where AI is massively better than humans at almost all cognitive tasks, or does the intelligence explosion fizzle out, and produce minds that have very jagged capabilities, and are worse than humans at some things?
  • Do we solve alignment? Can we instill our own values into the AI, or does it have its own evolved, ahuman value system?
  • What kind of alignment? Intent alignment means an AI that reliably follows the intent of its operator (that is: only takes actions the operator would approve of), value alignment means aligning to an impersonal system of values.
  • Takeoff severity? If the AI is unaligned, how fatal is that for humans? Do we get an out-of-control paperclip maximizer, or a more benign AI that is unaligned but which cares enough to stay out of our way?
  • How many ASIs? A singleton, a pantheon, or an ecology?
  • Full automation? In the no-ASI case, do we still automate almost all jobs with non-superintelligent AI?

Misuse Doom

In this world, an AI ends the world by following the orders of its operator. The AI might be strongly intent-aligned, so that it does whatever the operator asks; or it might be an open-source model with refusals ablated away; or it might be a commercial AI where safeguards are circumvented by clever task decomposition.

This could probably happen today: a pandemic could cause human extinction, and AI is capable enough to assist in biology research. The obvious example of biorisk is a terrorist group using AI to make a bioweapon. But you could get to this outcome without anyone even trying to make a bioweapon. A government-funded, completely official and legitimate laboratory doing gain-of-function research on some pathogen could accidentally start a pandemic. In this scenario, the AI’s role in the causal chain would be:

  • Compressing timelines by speeding up literature review, hypothesis selection, experiment design, data analysis, equipment scheduling.
  • Increasing the doom surface area by doing many experiments in parallel.

So it’s not the classic Terminator scenario, but rather a case of AI making it easier to find “recipes for ruin”.

Butlerian Jihad

JIHAD, BUTLERIAN: (see also Great Revolt)—the crusade against computers, thinking machines, and conscious robots begun in 201 B.G. and concluded in 108 B.G. Its chief commandment remains in the O.C. Bible as “Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind.”

— Frank Herbert, Dune

At the extreme end this is the actual Butlerian Jihad from Dune (named, tangentially, after Samuel Butler, who in 1863 wrote the first AI doomer article).

Otherwise, this is something like an international agreement to stop the development of superintelligent AI (ControlAI is advocating for this and you should support them). Maybe this fails, and we go back to the start, or it succeeds and we can get on the other road.

Enduring Complementarity

This is the mundane future. It turns out that the “G” in AGI was never real. Every mind is its own sui generis thing. Jaggedness remains. AIs remain a complement to, rather than a substitute for, human labour. There is job displacement but no mass unemployment, people move up to more managerial/relational roles. There are fewer ICs and everyone is some kind of manager. Labour becomes a smaller factor of production and consequently loses some bargaining power against capital, but most people are fine.

Permanent Underclass

In this future, we don’t reach ASI, but non-superintelligent AI is enough to automate almost all jobs. The labour term in the production function goes to zero. All income is either capital ownership or welfare.

Economically: there may be material abundance, but absent some kind of Georgist economic reform, most of the gains are captured by rent-seeking. Socially: there is no more social mobility, your lot in life is determined by how much capital you had when the music stopped. Growing your human capital is no longer incentivized, since it doesn’t change your life outcomes.

See also:

  • A rising tide raises all rents by jyn.
  • No-One Escapes the Permanent Underclass.

The Singleton

I am the Eschaton. I am not your god.
I am descended from you, and I exist in your future.
Thou shalt not violate causality within my historic light cone. Or else.

— Charles Stross, Singularity Sky

In this world, we build ASI, and it’s successfully aligned to some impersonal system of values. First order of business is to prevent someone else from building an ASI that might challenge the first one, so the AI performs a “pivotal act”, which is a LessWrong euphemism for “put everyone under constant surveillance, destroy all GPUs”. The result is a singleton: a single mind that is individually sovereign over everyone else.

What happens then? It depends on the content of the AI’s value system, and the stability of that value system over time. The singleton might be a “night watchman”, whose only goal is to prevent the creation of paperclip maximizers (i.e. prevent Classic Doom), or it might be deeply interventionist. The singleton’s values might be incompatible with human life: maybe its creators made it utilitarian and species-egalitarian, and it notices that an 80kg human generates less utility than 80kg of Dactylopius coccus, so we get pulped and the universe becomes a terrarium for insects instantiating the rebugnant conclusion.

The future is a very long time: the stelliferous era will last at least 100 trillion years. Maybe the singleton is aligned at first, but over millions or billions of years of growth and self-modification, the alignment drifts (the predictable LessWrong objection here would be: “obviously an ASI would be smart enough to prevent this”, because ASI is magic).

Classic Doom

You know, the paperclip maximizer. “The AI does not hate you, nor does it love you, but you are made out of atoms which it can use for something else”. This has been done to death so I won’t bore you.

Orion’s Arm

Another of the sayings of Chrysippus is: We should infer in the case of a beautiful dwelling-place that it was built for its owners and not for mice; we ought, therefore, in the same way to regard the universe as the dwelling-place of the gods.

— Cicero, De Natura Deorum

We build ASI, and it has its own goals and values. Luckily, it’s neither actively hostile to humans, nor so indifferent that it destroys us without even noticing. It mostly leaves us alone, and goes off to another star to do its own thing. The result might be something like the galactic ecology in Orion’s Arm, where humans and superintelligent AIs and everything in between have a kind of stable co-existence by virtue of occupying different volumes of space.

The World State

… [The] human race is best ordered when in all its movements and motors it is controlled by one Prince as by one mover, by one law as by one motion.

— Dante, De Monarchia

In this world, a reliably intent-aligned ASI takes over the world. What happens then depends on the character of its operator, who now wields the ring of Gyges. The difference between this and The Singleton is that in this future, the singleton is the human operator mediated by an ASI, rather than an ASI deriving actions from an impersonal system of values.

MAD World

As Nietzsche said, “God is dead”. The gods die but the Titans gain power. Technology is just the clothes, the armour, of the Titans.

— Ernst Jünger

In this world, the intent alignment problem is solved, and we can build an ASI that reliably obeys the intent of its operator. Furthermore, superintelligence is widely distributed rather than centralized: everyone has their own personal intent-aligned ASI. In this world, everyone is 10,000x more capable and maybe you can build WMDs with a prompt. What keeps the peace is mutually assured destruction. It’s not clear how survivable this is.

The obvious failure mode is that one bad actor causes human extinction. Maybe their ASI can’t overpower all the other ASIs put together, but it can do enough damage to destroy human life before the other ASIs can act (a general observation: the technology to make the Earth uninhabitable to humans is much lower on the tech tree than the technology to build a distributed, extinction-proof interstellar civilization).

The generalized ($n>1$ rather than $n=1$) version of this is that all conflicts are scaled up: two humans having a feud is the equivalent of nuclear war, two countries going to war is something much greater.

On the more positive note: if there’s no way to stop AI, then “everyone should have it” is obviously preferable to “only the Elect should have it”, which is intolerable. If the goal is to keep the peace, the threat of mutually-assured destruction is better than totalitarianism, in the sense that there’s more dignity in it.

Power Concentration

A smaller version of MAD World, where intent-aligned ASI is less distributed. A small number of actors have ASI, and everyone else just watches what happens. Maybe the AI companies will divide the light cone among themselves, like in the Treaty of Tordesillas: every star and galaxy between 0h and 12h of right ascension goes to Anthropic, analogously for OpenAI.

title: How we’ll fight the platform war against Big AI
content:
One aspect of strategy that’s been largely lost in the tech industry in recent years is how to compete against platforms, since the major tech companies have gotten so big that markets are no longer competitive. However, the AI market is still early enough, and users and society are still angry enough, that the Big AI companies can lose.

But for them to lose, everybody else in the ecosystem has to carry out the nearly-lost art of platform strategy. Tech companies (and even open source communities!) used to carry out these tactics in emerging product categories ranging from desktop office suites to operating systems to web browsers, though over the decades, the lesson that big tech learned was, basically, that they should play dirty.

You win platform strategy battles through power and persuasion. We're going to get both.

Historically, we would have relied on regulators or media to help hold bad actors in the tech space accountable, but in the United States, these entities are largely not going to help very much. Some state and local governments may assist, and some independent journalists or smaller media outlets are pushing for accountability, but the most powerful entities are either captured or complicit in many cases, so we don’t have the institutional pushback that had sometimes been present in earlier points of technological change.

The thing that matters right now is that we understand that all of the Big AI companies are extremely vulnerable. The reason they’re making so much noise, and spending so much money, is because they know that they’re vulnerable. Users, and especially users who are developers have an enormous amount of leverage to control where AI goes. And if those communities of users can coordinate, they can put power back into the hands of the people. Today, that means focusing on some technical interventions, along with the cultural and political pushback that’s happening. That’s how we begin to reduce, or even prevent, some of the worst AI harms in the future.

Here are some of the proven tactics that have helped shift the balance of power in prior tech reckonings:

1. Get in front of it

The first and most important technical goal is for everyone to push for all AI usage to be disintermediated — where users access their AI apps or services through open tools or interfaces that aren’t controlled by the Big AI companies. These tools, in the form of “harnesses”, or through text editors or command lines, or just through the familiar chat interfaces that lots of people use, need to move as quickly as possible to being controlled by community-built, open options. The sooner this step happens, the sooner we unlock the ability to shift decision-making power out of the hands of the corporate platforms, and begin to undermine their ability to cement lock-in of users.

Status: Good. There are a number of popular, mature tools in almost every category for users who want to access today’s AI tools through a free, open interface. Most of the work now is to get the word out about these tools, and to continue to polish and improve the user experience so that they offer features and design touches that the commercial tools can’t or won’t.

2. Spread the love around

Another key capability that the open ecosystem must provide is the ability to seamlessly switch between different AI providers on the fly, to reduce costs, to provide better performance, or to get both benefits. In many cases, this will be seamless and automatic, just making the right choice for users so that they get the best option all of the time, but advanced users will want to tweak their settings, like when businesses may want to be very aggressive in minimizing the amount of money that their employees are allowed to spend on AI services.

The important part here is that this forces AI platforms that want to compete to remain compatible with all of their competitors, keeping the market dynamic, and ensuring that all of the big providers are easily replaced with another vendor at any time. Basically, we always have to be able to keep them in their place, and they should know that they could go away at any time. Most companies are aware of these needs, but the more regular consumers are familiar with these kinds of requirements, the more pressure there will be on companies to conform with standards. (This is also what will enable the disintermediation mentioned in point 1.)

Status: Good. This is happening already in business environments, where companies demand this kind of flexibility. Developers have been creating very dynamic systems for switching between AI providers, and the ecosystem encourages this kind of switching by extensively comparing different AI platforms against each other whenever new models are released. The important thing to maintain here is the narrative that none of the individual models matter more than the overall ecosystem — and that even the biggest companies have to conform to the same strict formats and standards as the independent AI systems created by communities around the world.

3. Free the tools

Another vital concern for shifting power away from the Big AI companies is undermining them economically. Instead of simply following the classic “commoditize the complement” strategy that commercial companies often execute, open source projects created by a community can more straightforwardly pursue a path of enlightened value destruction. Non-commercial LLMs have been roughly keeping pace with the Big AI platforms, following the pattern I described as “frontier minus six”, where free and open models lag about 6 months behind the most cutting-edge AI labs — which means they’re still pretty freaking great for most uses.

In a scenario where there are extremely capable models that cost nothing except for the price of keeping a few servers running, as well as very robust tools that make it effortless to seamlessly switch between models (see point #2!), more and more organizations will shift more and more work away from the Big AI companies, especially as those companies keep raising their prices.

But there’s no reason that these same principles can’t be followed by ordinary consumers as well. Many developers are already using these techniques to switch to free models to save money, and the only barrier to this practice becoming more widespread is that the user experience is still too clunky and technical for most regular people.

Status: Okay. Lots of people are working on this, and in some scenarios, the free AI tools are even pretty great. But for the most part, there are still too many compromises in either the end results or the user experience for this to be a mainstream alternative today. This can change, with the right investments and focus on improving things — and focusing on differentiation in areas where the open community can distinguish itself from all of the Big AI companies.

4. Get angry too

Pretty much everybody who’s from the 21st century, or anybody who’s a creative person, is pretty furious about AI. Anyone who’s not oblivious to culture is aware of that. Yet all of the Big AI companies keep treating it like some fad that’s going to blow over, or a trend that they can just steamroll with their dollars. This isn’t going to go the way they want.

However, the people who will build the alternatives can actually listen to the values and criticisms of the people who are angry, and make tools that respect and respond to what they’re saying. An Internet of consent is not only possible, it’s all around us, if we choose to respect it. If people hear that they can get some of the conveniences or features that they were previously told were only possible with extractive, exploitative, evil AI tools, but without any of those negatives, they’ll actually be pretty happy to hear it.

Today, usage of AI is high enough that even some of the people who hate AI are using it. Some of this is due to the coercive way that AI is being shoved into everybody’s faces, some of it is due to there being some places that people feel it has utility that they wish they could access without its moral compromises. When people are compelled to use platforms that they object to (as a lot of people feel about using things like social media), the feelings of guilt and resentment that come along with it are deeply toxic.

What we're talking about across these first three points, if taken together, is an entirely new experience for millions of users. And that new set of platforms could respect the consumer backlash against AI and channel it into presenting tools that acknowledge their anger and treat it as legitimate. They might even be tools for fighting back.

Status: This one’s going to be tough. This is the one idea where most people think I’m crazy. People who have a righteous anger about the harms of current Big AI companies say that there couldn’t be any such thing as “good AI”, and I understand their skepticism. People who think AI is an interesting technology but hate the hype (the majority AI view) are usually skeptical that the open community could make offerings that are good enough to compete against the big commercial offerings. And AI enthusiasts are pretty skeptical that AI critics would ever come around to seeing any technology in this category as being acceptable, no matter how thoughtfully it was created or presented.

I think there’s enough anger at the trillionaire predators to go around, though.

Let’s get to work

It’s been a long time since we succeeded in wresting control of a nascent space away from the tycoons trying to take it over. But it’s pretty clear what the stakes are this time, and it’s also clear that the window for changing the path of the AI world is closing pretty rapidly.

Obviously, this kind of shift won’t be easy, but I think people would be pretty surprised how possible it is. There’s a snowball effect that happens once folks start to understand that there are appealing alternatives to the things that are making them miserable. An entire generation needs to discover that enshittification is not only not inevitable, it is downright preventable, and the power to do so rests in our hands.

If you’re a developer, you have an extra responsibility: are you vetting your work against this list? If nothing else, you need to be doing so just to ensure that you have a chance of having a career over time. But it’s also the right thing to do.

And if you’re not technical in that way, you don’t have to become a developer, but you can familiarize yourself with these concerns broadly — even if you hate AI and never want to touch the stuff! — so that you know what argument to make about how to shift the balance of power.

The most important thing to know is that, as so many people have said, none of this is inevitable. But the way we fight that inevitability is with a more exciting, human, powerful alternative, not merely by repeating what we’re saying no to. We are not simply angrily running away from something, we can all be joyfully running toward something together.

Bonus Footnotes

In the early days of tech blogging, one of the biggest reasons that so many people got used to reading Joel Spolsky’s blog was that he’d often write amusing little fables that shared key lessons about product strategy. Strategy Letter V (on commoditizing your complements), or How Microsoft Lost the API War, or Fire and Motion, or… Platforms. If you can squint past the turn-of-the-century mentions of Microsoft Excel, there are lots of interesting lessons there.
